extracted_by: hand, T-0290 — the Democrat read, August 1834
note: Vol. I No. 37, and the richest issue of the month by a wide margin. Page 3 column 3 is transcribed by the Tesseract fallback and is the cleanest advertising column in the four issues — whole sentences, whole names, whole addresses — which is why seven of these fifteen claims come out of it. The two that matter most are elsewhere: the North Pier under construction and the town's population, both on page 2 column 5, in a column interleaved line by line with two unrelated items.

claims.notes: THE NORTH PIER, UNDER CONSTRUCTION, IN THE PAPER'S OWN WORDS, AND THIS IS THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL CLAIM OF THE MONTH. What is being built in August 1834 is a pier running out from the north bank INTO THE LAKE and across the sand-bar that closes the river mouth, in the expectation that vessels of the largest class will then be able to enter the river. Everything the reconstruction shows at the river mouth — whether there is a pier there at the scene date, how far out it runs, what it is for — has a dated documentary answer here rather than an inferred one, eleven months before the scene. The work is superintended by a lieutenant (the Army engineer); his name is cut away and is NOT supplied. THE COLUMN IS INTERLEAVED LINE BY LINE with two other items — a chemical recipe beginning 'Take two parts' at line 2060 and a note on a schooner and her repairs — and the sixteen lines named here are the ones the harbour sentence can be followed through. Four lines inside the cited range are DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED as unattributable between the two streams: 2077 ('d piece of sand'), 2085 ('sand dollars in'), 2087 and 2089. Line 2085 in particular would read as an appropriation figure — '[thousand] dollars' — and attaching a sum of money to the harbour on a line that may belong to the schooner is exactly the kind of supply this project forbids.

claims.notes: THE TOWN'S FIVE TRUSTEES, ELECTED 11 AUGUST 1834. 'Monday last' is fixed to the date by the election notice this corpus already carries: 'An Election will be held on Monday, the eleventh day of August next, at the Mansion [House] (E. H. Hadduck's), for the election of [trustees] for the Town of Chicago, for one [year]', By order of the Board of Trustees, Th. J. V. Owen Pres't (1834-07-30, claim c003; reprinted 1834-08-06, page 3, column 5). So this is the result of that poll, and Chicago's governing body for the year that ENDS in the summer of the scene date is on record by name. THREE NAMES ARE MINTED AND TWO ARE NOT. John H. Kinzie and J. K. Boyer are printed whole. 'S. C. Hogan' is read '[J.] S. C. Hogan' because this same issue advertises 'J. S. C. HOGAN' over a South Water Street store (claim c013) — a supply from the same issue, which is the strongest kind available here, and it is bracketed all the same. The other two are REFUSED: 'G[…]bard' is cut through the middle and 'Ebenezer G[…]' loses its surname at the column edge. Both have obvious candidates in this town and neither is written down, because a trustee of Chicago invented from four letters would be indistinguishable afterwards from one that was read.

claims.notes: A POPULATION FIGURE FOR THE TOWN, PRINTED, ELEVEN MONTHS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE: 'a population of over two t[housand two hun]dred'. The supply is bracketed and it is the only part of the sentence that is supplied — 'over two t' and 'dred' are the two surviving pieces, and 'two hundred' is the reading the fragment 'dred' will carry; a reader who prefers 'over two t[housand … hun]dred' loses nothing that matters, because the order of magnitude is what the claim is for. Beside it the paper lists what the town HAS in August 1834, and every item is a thing the reconstruction draws or decides not to draw: a garrison of troops, public works in progress (the harbour of claim c001), and the Indian Agency negotiating a treaty ratification. The complaint itself is about the mail — Chicago has no semi-daily mail where smaller places do — which is the same grievance the Democrat printed on 1834-08-06 about its own papers reaching subscribers late.

This is the editor arguing a case and it is read as such: what the claim carries is that the Democrat PRINTED these figures on 1834-08-13, not that twelve is the true count. claims.notes: RULING 3's VETO, FIRED ON A FIRM INSIDE THE MONTH BEING READ. Marsh & Simons is dissolved by mutual consent on 6 August 1834, and the notice runs a week later. The claim carries `contradicts`, which is what stops the partnership standing in the 1835 town as a documented business: a firm that the papers say ended is not furniture for the scene date, however well attested it was before. The surviving half of the concern is claim c006 — Edward Simons carries on alone at the Boston Market — and it is a SEPARATE business rather than a renaming, because the advertisement itself separates them.

claims.notes: THE BOSTON MARKET IS A NAMED PLACE OF BUSINESS IN CHICAGO IN AUGUST 1834, and Edward Simons keeps it on after the dissolution of claim c005. What the reconstruction can take from it is a TRADE and a NAME, not a position: 'the Boston Market' is stated as somewhere the citizens already know how to find, which is exactly the kind of address this town's advertising gives and exactly why the placement is `relative` on the market itself rather than on a street. A market selling provisions is a shopfront with a very particular look — open front, hanging meat, a block — and it is the first one this corpus has documented by name.

claims.notes: A BUILDING RAISED ON RANDOLPH STREET, DATED. 'they have erected a large and commodious building, for a shop, on Randolph street' is a construction event with a street, a use and a week — and 'large and commodious' is the paper's own account of its size, which is as much as a carriage shop's massing can be documented to. A carriage and sleigh shop needs a wide door and a yard, so this is a frontage that does not look like a dry-goods store's. THE SAME FIRM ADVERTISED DIFFERENTLY A WEEK EARLIER: on 1834-08-06 (page 4, column 1) the trade is announced 'on So[uth Water street?]' with the line cut, and here the new building is on Randolph. Both printings stand with their dates and neither overwrites the other, per the reading rule; whether it is a move or a second premises is not settled by either.

claims.notes: A CORNER, NAMED BY BOTH ITS STREETS: the Tin, Sheet Iron and Copper Factory at the corner of Lake and Dearborn. That is one of the two placement classes this project can put on the ground, and it is the strongest address in the month. What stands there is a WORKSHOP that also retails — tinsmithing, mending and jobbing, milk pans by the dozen — and it buys in barter: ginseng by the thousand pounds, raccoon and deer skins, old pewter, copper and brass, rags. A tin factory taking a ton of dried ginseng over the counter is the fur-trade economy still running underneath a retail town, and it is the sort of thing a card at this corner should say. 'Redcoat Deer Skins' is read 'R[ac]coo[n and] Deer Skins'; the same firm's advertising elsewhere in the month prints the trade goods list again but no cleaner.

claims.notes: THE POST OFFICE IS ON SOUTH WATER STREET, and this advertisement is what says so. Hogan places his own store 'in South Water Street, one [door] … the Post Office' — the direction word (east or west) is lost with the column and is NOT supplied, which is why the placement is `relative` on the post office rather than on a corner. Two things fall out of it for the reconstruction. First, a documented storefront on the town's principal street, with its trade: dry goods, groceries, hardware, crockery and glass. Second, the position of the POST OFFICE itself, which is a public building the scene has to place and which nothing in this corpus had located before. The same standing advertisement runs a week later (1834-08-20, claim c006 there) with 'the Post Office,' on its own line again, so the relationship is printed twice. J. S. C. Pierce & French take over a shop 'formerly occupied by … Abbott' — a building that changes hands rather than a new one, which is the kind of chain the ticket asks to be caught. Here the line ends at 'the corner of Lak[e'; on 1834-08-20 the same standing advertisement prints 'and Canel streets, opp[osite …] pied by Pierce and Abb[ott]' (page 4, column 5, lines 4429-4430, claim c007 there). The two printings disagree on that and both are recorded; 'the old shop formerly occupied by' is what this issue prints and 'opposite' is what the next one prints, and neither is preferred.

claims.notes: A STORE STOCKED OFF A NAMED VESSEL. The schooner Huron clears for St. Joseph in the Marine List of 1834-08-06 (claim c001 there), and here she is the ship that brought John Wright his spring and summer goods — the supply chain of a Chicago storefront, printed at both ends. The advertisement gives no address beyond 'his Store', so the placement is `none`; what it gives is the stock, which is the ordinary general assortment of this town in 1834 and is worth having as a baseline against which the specialists (the tin factory, the book store, the market) can be read as unusual.
